title: Carding the Cotton
summary: Cotton is carded again and again, down to fibre and fibre into fibre, until what remains is partless and is taken into emptiness; Heruka is not found, there is nothing to meditate on, on the broad road not a hair's tip enters, and there is no effect and cause. Munidatta reads the carding as an analysis of body, speech and mind in which the supposed whole is broken into parts and atoms until it is shown to be partless, the empty as the clear light the mind is made to enter, and the road as the nondual path (cp.26.m2, cp.26.m3, cp.26.m4); the Tibetan translation renders the carding itself as examination by valid cognition.

flags.note: The heading names only the rāga. The poet's name comes from the attribution śāntipādānām, 'of Śāntipāda', which Shastri prints before the song (removed from line 1a as not part of the verse). The Tibetan heading agrees: sha ba ri zhes bya ba'i glu dbyangs zhi ba'i zhabs kyi'o, 'the melody called Sha ba ri, of Zhi ba'i zhabs (Śāntipāda)'.

lines.gloss: cotton · having carded · having carded · into (to) fibre · fibre

flags.note: ām̐sure ām̐su is taken as 'fibre into fibre', with -re as the dative-locative ending: the cotton is carded down to fibre, and the fibre into finer fibre. 'Fibre after fibre' or 'fibre from fibre' are also possible. The line has no finite verb: dhuṇi dhuṇi is a repeated absolutive ('having carded and carded') and the subject is unstated, so the English uses participles.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) does not keep the image: tshad mas brtags shing brtags pa'i cha shas cha, 'examined and examined by valid cognition, the parts of what is examined, part'. It has tshad ma ('valid cognition, measure') for tulā, as if from tulā 'balance'; brtags ('examined') for dhuṇi; and cha shas ('part') for ām̐su, as if aṃśa. The English keeps the cotton and the carding.
Shastri's footnote records that the song has tulā (তুলা) where the commentary cites tula (তুল). The difference does not change the sense; see the witness note on this line.

lines.gloss: fibre · having carded · having carded · partless (? Munidatta: niravayava) · what remains (or: at the end)

flags.note: ṇirabara is of uncertain derivation. Munidatta cites it as niravara and explains it as niravayava, 'partless' (cp.26.m2); the glossary rendering follows him. The Tibetan line, cha shas cha shas brtags na lhag ma med, 'when part and part are examined, there is no remainder', covers ṇirabara sesu together with lhag ma med, which would make the line say 'nothing is left'.
sesu is taken as śeṣa, 'what remains', the subject of the clause. It could also be a locative, 'at the end' ('at the end it is partless').

lines.gloss: and so, therefore (?) · Heruka (? see flag) · not · is found

flags.note: herua is read as Heruka, the deity: Apabhraṃśa regularly loses a k between vowels (heruka > herua), and the glossary records the same form in song 17's heruabīṇā, 'Heruka's vīṇā'. Neither old witness reads Heruka here. The Tibetan line has gzugs, 'form' (de nyid phyir na gzugs ni ma rnyed do, 'for that very reason form is not found'), perhaps hearing rua, Apabhraṃśa for rūpa, in the word. Munidatta's paraphrase has hetvantara, 'another cause': since that mind is without cause, no other cause of it is found (cp.26.m2), as if he heard hetu (Prakrit heu). Old Bengali her-, 'look', would give 'looked for, it is not found' or 'nothing to be seen is found'. Heruka is chosen as the plain sense of the printed form; the reviewer should decide.
tauṣe is taken as 'and so, therefore', with the Tibetan de nyid phyir na. 'Even so, still' is possible and would change the logic of the refrain.

lines.gloss: Śānti · says · what · that, it (?) · is meditated on
lines.en: [Śāntipāda]{p-santi} says: what is there to meditate on?

flags.note: Shastri prints kiṇa sabhābi ai. Read here as kiṇa sa bhābiai, with bhābiai a passive in -iai ('is meditated on, is brought into being') that rhymes with pābiai in 2a. Munidatta's paraphrase, kiṃ bhāvyate, 'what is meditated on?' (cp.26.m2), and the Tibetan line, shAn+tis smras pa ci zhig sgom par byed, 'Śānti says: what does one meditate on?', agree. Dividing sabhāba, 'nature' (svabhāva), would give something like 'what nature is there?'.
The poet names himself Sānti, without the honorific -pāda. The glossary rendering Śāntipāda is used, as the drafting rules require; see questions.

lines.gloss: cotton · having carded · having carded · in (into) the empty, emptiness · (I) took, brought (?)
lines.en: [Carding]{dhuni}, carding the [cotton]{tula}, I took it into [emptiness]{sunyata};

flags.note: ahāriu is uncertain. It is taken from āhṛ, 'take, bring', in line with Munidatta's praveśitaṃ mayā, 'I made (the mind) enter' (cp.26.m3). A link with āhāra, 'food' ('I consumed it in the empty'), is possible. The Tibetan line, tshad mas brtags brtags stong pa nyid du song, has 'examined and examined by valid cognition, it went into emptiness'.

The -iu form is taken as a first-person past, so 'I' is supplied, as in Munidatta's mayā (cp.26.m3); 'it' (the cotton) is supplied as the object. The Tibetan reads the verb as intransitive ('it went'). sune is the locative of suna (śūnya), 'in the empty', rendered 'into emptiness'.

lines.gloss: again · having taken · (one's) own self · (I) stopped, did away with (?)
lines.en: taking it up again, I put a stop to my own self.

flags.note: caṭāriu is obscure. It is rendered 'put a stop to' because the two witnesses agree: Munidatta, citing the word as caṭāriva, says that self-grasping in the form of object of meditation and meditator is refuted or annulled (bādhita) (cp.26.m3), and the Tibetan line has slar yang blangs nas rang gi 'gog par byed, 'taking up again, one stops one's own'. A literal sense such as 'cracked' or 'scattered' cannot be ruled out.
apaṇā is taken as the object, 'one's own self' (the Tibetan has rang gi); it could instead mean 'by myself'. 'It' in 'taking it up again' is supplied; Munidatta makes it the clear light (cp.26.m3).

lines.translit: bahala baṭa dui māra na diśaa
lines.gloss: broad, thick (or: flowing?) · road · two · Māra(s) (or: killers?) · not · is seen
lines.en: On the broad [road]{road} two [Māra]{mara}s are not seen;

flags.note: dui māra is read as 'two Māras', māra being the word for Māra in song 16. Alternatives: 'two killers', the literal sense of the word, robbers absent from a safe road, as toll station and guard post are absent from the road of song 15; Munidatta's dual aspect (dvayākāra): on this excellent path, being nondual, the dual aspect does not exist (cp.26.m4); and the Tibetan line's rnam pa gnyis, 'two aspects' or 'two kinds' (rnam pa gnyis 'bab lam ni ma mthong ste). Neither witness has Māra (the Tibetan word for Māra is bdud). Their agreement might point to a text with ākāra, 'aspect', here; that is only a guess.

Munidatta cites the first word as vahala (vahaletyādi, cp.26.m4), and the Tibetan line has 'bab, 'descend, flow', as if from vah-, 'flow, carry'; Bengali script does not separate b and v. Shastri's bahala is read as 'broad, thick' (Sanskrit bahala).

lines.gloss: Śānti · says · hair's tip · not · enters

flags.note: What the hair's tip does not enter is unstated, presumably the broad road of 4a. The Tibetan line, shAn+tis smras pa skra rtse'i cha mi shong, has 'not a hair-tip's portion has room'. Munidatta first takes bāla as 'fool' (cp.26.m4); see the notes.
Śāntipāda for the poet's Śānti, as in 2b.

lines.gloss: effect, work · not · cause · this (?) · in the world (?)
lines.en: In this world there is no [effect and cause]{karya-karana};

flags.note: jaehu jaati is uncertain. It is taken as 'in this world', with jaati from jagati (Prakrit loses the g) and jaehu as a demonstrative; 'whatever is born' (jāti, 'birth') is another possibility. The Tibetan line, bya ba byed pa zung dag yod ma yin, 'act and agent: the pair does not exist', has 'pair' (zung dag) and no world. Munidatta's paraphrase does not take up the two words (cp.26.m5).
The single na is taken to deny both, 'neither effect nor cause'; the glossary pair 'effect and cause' is kept as one phrase in the English.

sam̐em̐ sam̐beaṇa is taken as one instrumental phrase, 'by self-awareness' (svasaṃvedana), as in the Tibetan rang gis rig pas shAn+ti pa yis smras, 'Śāntipa spoke by self-awareness'. Read as svayam, 'oneself', and saṃvedana, 'knowing', the line could mean 'Śānti speaks of what is known by oneself'.
Śāntipāda for the poet's Sānti, as in 2b.

notes.text: Rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music. Each song is headed by the rāga to which it is sung, here Śīvarī. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) transcribes the name sha ba ri, which points rather to a form like Śabarī or Śavarī; which spelling is original is uncertain.

Munidatta introduces the song: the siddha master Śānti, his heart soaked with the fullness of delight in the joy of knowledge, sets out that same meaning for the sake of people (cp.26.m1). The Tibetan has 'filled and moistened with the bliss of the joy of knowledge'.

The poet names himself in the refrain (2b, Sānti) and in couplets 4 and 5 (4b, Śānti; 5b, Sānti); Shastri's spelling varies between s and ś. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) transcribes the name in the lines (shAn+ti, shAn+ti pa) and translates it in the heading as zhi ba'i zhabs, zhi ba being 'peace'. The English uses the glossary's Śāntipāda.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) turns the carding into examination throughout: tulā becomes tshad ma, 'valid cognition' or 'measure'; dhuṇi becomes brtags, 'examined'; ām̐su becomes cha shas, 'part' (1a: tshad mas brtags shing brtags pa'i cha shas cha; 1b: cha shas cha shas brtags na lhag ma med; 3a: tshad mas brtags brtags stong pa nyid du song). These are readings, not the image, and the English keeps the cotton. The Tibetan comment on couplet 1 still transcribes the cited word as tu la.

Carding is the beating or combing of raw cotton to loosen it and separate its fibres before spinning (Old Bengali dhuṇi, 'having carded'). The song has the cotton carded again and again, down to fibre and the fibre into finer fibre, until what remains is partless (1b); couplet 3 returns to the same work.

Shastri's footnote records that the song has tulā (তুলা) where the commentary cites tula (তুল). Munidatta's citation of couplet 3 reads tuladhuṇītyādi, with a short a (cp.26.m3); his citation of couplet 1, tuletyādi (cp.26.m2), could stand for either form, since tula or tulā joined to ityādi both give tuletyādi. Both are taken as the same word, cotton (Sanskrit tūla).

Munidatta reads couplet 1 as an argument about parts and wholes. Playing on tulā, 'balance', he calls body, speech and mind, the three worlds, 'fit for weighing' (tulanayogya) because of the faults of nature. Speaking in the poet's voice, he says he has proved that the part has six parts, against a whole (avayavin) taken as one by a single valid cognition despite distinctions such as moving and unmoving; the atoms of the heap that makes up the parts are shaken again and again (dhūtvā dhūtvā) through their six-partedness, and the whole is shown to be partless (niravayava). (The Sanskrit ṣaḍaṅgatābhāvena can be divided either as 'through having six parts' or 'through the absence of six parts'; the Tibetan has 'divided again and again into six parts, as without entity'.) He closes by referring to a 'chapter on wisdom' (prajñāpariccheda) for a passage beginning 'when examined' (cp.26.m2).

ṇirabara: Munidatta cites it as niravara and explains it as niravayava, 'partless' (cp.26.m2), the glossary rendering; the Old Bengali derivation is unclear. sesu is taken as śeṣa, 'what remains'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) renders the phrase lhag ma med, 'without remainder', which would make the line say that nothing is left.

herua is read here as Heruka, the wrathful deity of the yoginī tantras: Apabhraṃśa regularly loses a k between vowels (heruka > herua), and the glossary records the same form in heruabīṇā, 'Heruka's vīṇā', in song 17. Neither old witness reads Heruka here. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de nyid phyir na gzugs ni ma rnyed do, 'for that very reason form is not found', perhaps hearing rua, the Apabhraṃśa form of rūpa, 'form', in the word. Munidatta's paraphrase has hetvantara, 'another cause': since that mind is without cause, no other cause of it is found (cp.26.m2), as if he heard hetu, 'cause' (Prakrit heu). A link with Old Bengali her-, 'look', would give 'looked for, it is not found' or 'nothing to be seen is found'.

Munidatta ties the refrain to his argument: since that mind is without cause, no other cause of it is found (hetvantaraṃ na prāpyate), words that stand where the song has herua ṇa pābiai; and Śāntipāda says that, since there is no apprehension of things (bhāvopalambha), nothing is meditated on (kiṃ bhāvyate) (cp.26.m2). The Tibetan comment agrees in substance: 'free of cause' (rgyu dang bral ba) and 'what is to be meditated on?' (ci zhig bsgom par bya).

sune is the locative of suna (śūnya), 'empty', rendered 'into emptiness'. ahāriu is uncertain: from āhṛ, 'take, bring', as rendered, or from āhāra, 'food', 'consumed'. Munidatta's gloss on the line is 'I have made the mind enter clear light' (cp.26.m3); the Tibetan line has 'examined and examined by valid cognition, it went into emptiness' (stong pa nyid du song).

caṭāriu is obscure. Munidatta cites it as caṭāriva and explains the line with bādhita, 'refuted, annulled' (cp.26.m3); the Tibetan line and comment have 'gog pa, 'stopping, blocking'. 'Put a stop to' follows what the two share. apaṇā is the reflexive 'one's own (self)'.

Munidatta calls couplet 3 his 'second verse' (he does not count the refrain), which makes the same point firm. The carding is examination by valid cognition, drawing out the parts and the rest (dattvā; the Tibetan has 'byin pa, 'extracting'). On 'empty' (śūnya) he has the poet say: 'I have made the mind enter clear light.' On caṭāriu, cited as caṭāriva, he says that, once that clear light is taken up, the form of self-grasping, as object of meditation and meditator, is refuted (bādhita). He quotes the Dvikalpa (Hevajra): 'there is no meditator, nor anything to be meditated on' (nāsti bhāvako na bhāvyo 'sti) (cp.26.m3).

dui māra is read as 'two Māras': māra is the songs' word for Māra, the tempter (song 16). It may instead mean 'killers', the literal sense of the name; the road would then be free of robbers, as the road of song 15 is free of toll stations and guard posts. Munidatta's paraphrase has the dual aspect (dvayākāra) in its place: on this excellent path, being nondual, the dual aspect does not exist (cp.26.m4). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) goes with him: rnam pa gnyis 'bab lam ni ma mthong ste, roughly 'the descending road of the two aspects is not seen' (the syntax is unclear); it has no bdud, its word for Māra. The first word, bahala, 'broad, thick', is cited by Munidatta as vahala, and the Tibetan 'bab, 'descend, flow', suggests vah-, 'flow, carry'.

Munidatta introduces couplet 4, his 'third verse', as praise of the path: because the path is nondual, the dual aspect does not exist on it. He reads bālāga in two ways: first as bāla, 'fool', the ignorant one who does not enter this dharma and stays far from it; or else as 'like a hair' (bālavat): here there is not even the joint of a line. He quotes a verse of Nāgārjunapāda beginning sauśīryante kāye, which the Tibetan renders de yi lus la khong seng med, 'in that body there is no hollow' (cp.26.m4).

The Tibetan translation's line (Toh 2293) has skra rtse'i cha mi shong, 'not a hair-tip's portion has room'. Its comment keeps the hair in both of Munidatta's readings and has no fool: 'if one enters here by way of a hair-tip's portion, that too is far'; 'or else, there is no portion of the joint of a hair's tip here' (cp.26.m4).

kāja is Sanskrit kārya, 'work, effect', set against kāraṇa, 'cause'. jaehu jaati is uncertain; 'in this world' takes jaati from jagati. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has bya ba byed pa zung dag yod ma yin, 'act and agent: the pair does not exist', with zung dag, 'pair', where the Bengali has jaehu jaati. Munidatta's comment does not take up the two words (cp.26.m5).

Munidatta introduces couplet 5, his 'fourth verse', as stating the apprehension of the true nature (svarūpopalambha), after the refrain's absence of any apprehension of things (cp.26.m2). Śānti, himself free of effect and cause, speaks the unsurpassed state; this reasoning is established by valid cognition, and by the true guru's grace the unsurpassed state is known by oneself. He quotes the Dvikalpa: it is known by oneself, from merit, through serving the succession of gurus (cp.26.m5).

termsOmitted.reason: Hit in the Tibetan line only (cha shas, 'part'), where the Bengali has ām̐su, 'fibre'; the English follows the Bengali image (amsu forbids 'part' in a verse line).
Hit in the Tibetan line only (tshad ma), which stands for the Bengali tulā, 'cotton'; a reading, not in the Bengali. See the witness note on cp.26.
Hit in the Tibetan line only (cha shas, 'part'), for the Bengali ām̐su, 'fibre'.
Hit in the Tibetan line (sgom pa). The Bengali bhābiai is rendered by the verb 'meditate on'; the glossary rendering is the noun 'meditation', so it is not marked.
Hit in the Tibetan line only (tshad ma), for the Bengali tulā, 'cotton'; a reading, not in the Bengali.

proposals.definition: A 'chapter on wisdom' (prajñā, 'wisdom'; pariccheda, 'section, chapter') that Munidatta cites at the end of his comment on the first couplet of song 26, for a passage beginning vicārite, 'when examined' (cp.26.m2); the Tibetan has shes rab le'u. He does not name the work, and the phrase may describe a chapter rather than give a title.
proposals.rationale: Munidatta cites it as a source, as he cites a 'Chapter on Empowerment' (tx-sekapatala). An entry lets the reviewer identify the work once; it may be the wisdom chapter of the Bodhicaryāvatāra, which he quotes in song 6, but that is unchecked.

proposals.definition: A cause (hetu), above all the direct cause from which an effect arises, as against its supporting conditions. Munidatta says that what has been shown to be partless has no cause, so no other cause (hetvantara) of that mind is found (cp.26.m2), words that stand where song 26 (2a) has herua. The Tibetan has rgyu.
proposals.rationale: A basic term of Munidatta's causal arguments, distinct from kāraṇa (glossary 'effect and cause'), and needed to discuss his paraphrase of 2a. The Tibetan rgyu is left out of the match forms, since the glossary also uses rgyu for 'warp' (song 25) and it occurs inside rgyud.

questions: 2a herua: I put Heruka in the line, as the regular Apabhraṃśa form of heruka (the form of song 17's heruabīṇā), although the Tibetan line has gzugs, 'form', Munidatta paraphrases with hetvantara, 'another cause', and Old Bengali her-, 'look', is also possible. Do you accept Heruka, or prefer 'form', 'cause' or a 'look' reading? If Heruka stands, should p-heruka be matched here (the hit detector skipped it)?

Related to 2a: m3 cites the Dvikalpa only by its opening, nāsti bhāvako na bhāvyo 'sti. From memory, not from the pack, the Hevajra verse goes on to deny mantra and deity; if so, it would support Heruka in 2a. Please check the Hevajra before relying on this.

4a dui māra: I chose 'two Māras' and tagged mara. Would you rather have 'two killers' (robbers absent from the road, as toll station and guard post are absent in song 15), or a reading after Munidatta's 'dual aspect' and the Tibetan 'two aspects', which may reflect a text with ākāra? And should bahala be 'broad' (Shastri) or 'flowing' (Munidatta's vahala, the Tibetan 'bab)?
3b caṭāriu: 'I put a stop to my own self' rests on the agreement of Munidatta (bādhita) and the Tibetan ('gog pa). Do you know a literal Old Bengali sense (crack, scatter?) that should replace it?
3a ahāriu: 'I took it into emptiness' (āhṛ, with Munidatta's praveśitaṃ mayā), or 'I consumed it' (āhāra)? Is the supplied first person acceptable, given that the Tibetan has 'it went'?
1b ṇirabara sesu: 'what remains is partless' (Munidatta's niravayava, the glossary term) or 'nothing is left' (the Tibetan lhag ma med)?
2b: may I divide kiṇa sa bhābiai (a passive rhyming with pābiai, as Munidatta's kiṃ bhāvyate and the Tibetan sgom pa suggest) against Shastri's kiṇa sabhābi ai?

5a jaehu jaati: 'in this world' (jaati < jagati) is a guess, and the Tibetan has 'the pair does not exist'. Do you have a better parse? Also, the glossary pair 'effect and cause' makes 'there is no effect and cause' a little stiff; would you accept 'neither effect nor cause' as a variant?
The poet calls himself Sānti or Śānti in 2b, 4b and 5b; the glossary's English is Śāntipāda, which I used as the rules require. May 'Śānti' be added as a variant of p-santi for the self-naming lines?

m2's 'chapter on wisdom' (prajñāpariccheda; Tibetan shes rab le'u), cited for a passage beginning vicārite: is it the wisdom chapter of the Bodhicaryāvatāra, which Munidatta quotes in song 6? I proposed tx-prajnapariccheda without identifying it.
